definition: Stingy means unwilling to spend or give money, holding tightly to every cent.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word stingy. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know stingy should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Everyone enjoyed dinner with Uncle Ray until the check arrived, because he was famously stingy and would study the bill for ten minutes rather than leave a fair tip.
A frugal person spends carefully and hates waste, while a stingy person refuses to spend or give even when fairness calls for it.
A stingy person grips their money tightly, but a miserly one hoards it obsessively while living as though they had nothing.

Tightfisted pictures a hand gripping money so it cannot escape: reluctant to spend on anyone, including yourself. Stingy covers the same unwillingness to spend or give but adds a social sting; it is the word people reach for when someone will not pay a fair share.

Cheap, applied to a person, means dodging spending even when fairness calls for it: splitting a bill down to the penny, skipping the tip. It is the most casual and cutting of these words. Stingy is the slightly more general term for being unwilling to spend or give.

Penny-pinching describes fussy, small-scale economizing: counting out coupons, grudging every little expense. It highlights the pettiness of the savings. Stingy is broader and harsher: a stingy person is unwilling to spend or give at all, whether the amount is pennies or hundreds.
giving freely and willingly
giving readily, without holding back
Stingy's true origin is unproven, but the favorite theory ties it to sting, from Old English stingan — picturing someone so sharp and prickly about money that parting with a single cent stings.
Stingy means unwilling to spend or give money, holding tightly to every cent.
The office manager was so stingy with supplies that employees had to sign a form to receive a single new pen, and he kept the box of paper clips locked in his own desk drawer.
Rationing pens and locking up paper clips shows an unwillingness to spend or hand out even the tiniest amounts, which is exactly what makes the manager stingy.
Stingy is an everyday, mildly insulting word for someone unwilling to spend or give.
It describes habits with money and generosity, not physical sensations; a wasp's sharp jab is a sting, never stingy.
In formal writing, miserly or parsimonious strikes a more elevated tone.

The Harborview Gulls sold out every home game, yet the roster told another story.
Owner Del Roscoe was, in every player's telling, stingy: bonuses promised in spring quietly vanished by fall, and the team bus lost its heater two winters running.
Roscoe spared nothing on himself — courtside seats at away games, a new boat named for the team — which made the vanishing bonuses harder to forgive.
When the star pitcher left for a rival who simply paid what was owed, the local paper ran the numbers: the Gulls kept the league's highest ticket prices and its lowest payroll.
Fans began bringing signs that said PAY THE TEAM, and by August even the mayor had repeated the phrase.
